clue.text: Bread and water? That's hairy stuff?

parts.note: bread is slang for money, ready cash
a mere is a lake, a stretch of still water

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about bread and water, then a guess that it is something hairy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bread and water' looks like prison fare, but each word is a separate piece of slang or synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashmere is fine wool combed from the hair of Kashmir goats.

clue.text: Get into trouble with a sherry glass

parts.note: to cop it is British slang for getting punished or into trouble

explanation.surface: Someone lands in hot water over a sherry glass.
explanation.definitionFit: A copita is the tulip-shaped glass traditionally used in Spain for tasting sherry.

clue.text: Deliberately they wreck boats, sure to be scrapped

indicators.note: scrapping the words breaks them up so their letters can be rebuilt into something new

explanation.surface: A warning about people who wreck boats on purpose, sure to be scrapped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be scrapped' signals the anagram of BOATS and SURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Saboteurs are people who damage or destroy property on purpose.

clue.text: Post parcel of tights

parts.note: post is mail
a parcel or lot is a bundle of goods offered together, as at auction

explanation.surface: Sending tights off in a parcel through the post.
explanation.definitionFit: A maillot is the close-fitting tights worn by dancers and gymnasts; the word also means a one-piece swimsuit.

clue.text: Crusty riparian boat-enthusiast

explanation.surface: A grumpy riverbank character who loves boats.
explanation.walkthrough: Ratty is the water rat in Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows, who says there is nothing like messing about in boats.
explanation.definitionFit: Crusty and short-tempered are both irritable; the riverside rodent in a children's classic carries the same name.

clue.text: Plan is worked out in the personal column

indicators.note: worked out means the letters are reworked into a different order

explanation.surface: Someone drafting a plan for a small ad in the newspaper's personal column.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked out' turns PLANIS into the answer. The 'personal column' is not the newspaper section but the column in your own back.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinal describes the backbone, the vertebral column every body carries.

clue.text: No stamp, possibly, giving him more work

definitions.text: No stamp, possibly, giving him more work

indicators.note: possibly says these letters may be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: An unstamped letter means extra trouble for the person who delivers it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals the anagram of NO STAMP, and the whole clue describes the deliverer burdened by unstamped mail.
explanation.definitionFit: The letter carrier is the one who must collect the surcharge on an unstamped item.

clue.text: I sigh over Elimelech's wife

indicators.note: in a down clue, over means the words are turned upside down, read from bottom to top

parts.note: to moan is to sigh or groan

explanation.surface: Someone sighing about a figure from the Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns the whole run I MOAN backwards. In the Book of Ruth, Elimelech's wife is the mother-in-law of Ruth.
explanation.definitionFit: Naomi is the Old Testament woman married to Elimelech of Bethlehem.

clue.text: Manx race really twisting recently

indicators.note: twisting the letters bends them into a new order

parts.note: the TT, Tourist Trophy, is the motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: A motorcycle race on the Isle of Man with a really twisty course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twisting' shuffles TT and REALLY together. The Isle of Man TT is a famous road race for motorcycles.
explanation.definitionFit: Latterly means lately, in the recent period.

clue.text: Standard meeting-place for a female climber

parts.note: par is the standard or normal level
a venue is a place where people meet

explanation.surface: A standard meeting point for a woman who climbs mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'climber' is a social climber, not a mountaineer; the final E makes the word feminine.
explanation.definitionFit: A parvenue is a woman who has risen suddenly in wealth or status, an upstart.

clue.text: T Williams's desire, say, as excited strip-club patron

indicators.note: excited letters are stirred up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A tale of a seedy customer at a strip club, linked to a playwright.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' signals the anagram of STRIP-CLUB PATRON. Tennessee Williams wrote A Streetcar Named Desire, so Desire is a streetcar, an example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A streetcar or tram is a vehicle carrying the general public on fixed routes.

clue.text: Wholeheartedly, friend to young child

indicators.note: to here means the friend is added to the end of the child

parts.note: a tot is a small child
an ally is a friend or supporter

explanation.surface: Being a wholehearted friend to a small child.
explanation.definitionFit: Totally means completely, without reservation.

clue.text: Opening bat making five a prime error

indicators.note: opening means this piece starts the word, coming before the rest

parts.note: V is the Roman numeral for five

indicators.note: an error in the letters means they have gone wrong and are jumbled

explanation.surface: A cricket opening batsman makes five and then a big mistake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opening bat' suggests a cricket opener, but 'Opening' puts V first and the bat is the animal; 'error' turns A PRIME into AMPIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: The vampire bat is a blood-feeding bat of Central and South America.

clue.text: Meet county fellows

definitions.note: a meet is the gathering of riders and hounds before a hunt, so stands for the riders themselves

parts.note: Hunts is the abbreviation for Huntingdonshire, a former English county
fellows are men

explanation.surface: An invitation to meet the gentlemen of the county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Meet' looks like a verb but is the noun for an assembly of fox-hunters. Huntingdonshire was an English county, now part of Cambridgeshire.
explanation.definitionFit: Fox-hunting riders assemble at a meet, the collective gathering of hunt followers.

clue.text: Hating Dutch, we hear?

parts.note: my old Dutch is Cockney for a wife, so hating one's Dutch is reported as hating wives and wedlock

explanation.surface: A rumour that someone cannot stand the Dutch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dutch' looks like the nationality, but 'my old Dutch' (from duchess) is Cockney slang for a wife; 'we hear' marks it as what people say.
explanation.definitionFit: Misogamy is a hatred of marriage.

clue.text: Unknown to the Spanish, this post at end of flight

parts.note: something new to you is unknown to you
el is Spanish for the

explanation.surface: Something unfamiliar to Spaniards: a post at the end of a flight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' suggests air travel but is a flight of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A newel is the upright post at the top or foot of a staircase that supports the handrail.

clue.text: Was it re-shaped by policy of Banting?

definitions.text: Was it re-shaped by policy of Banting?

indicators.note: re-shaped means the letters are given a new form

parts.note: a line is a policy, as in the party line

explanation.surface: Asking whether a figure was slimmed by a dieting regime.
explanation.walkthrough: 're-shaped' gives WAIST from WAS IT. William Banting popularised a low-carbohydrate diet in Victorian England, so his policy would slim the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: The waistline is the measure round the middle that a diet aims to reduce.

clue.text: Hardtop vehicle at speed?

parts.note: a car is a vehicle
apace means quickly, at speed

explanation.surface: A hardtop car being driven fast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardtop' suggests a car roof, but here it is the hard upper shell of an animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A carapace is the hard upper shell of a tortoise or crab.

clue.text: Sea Change — work of early satirist

indicators.note: change means the letters are put in a different order

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

explanation.surface: A piece called Sea Change written by an early satirist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change' turns SEA into AES.
explanation.definitionFit: Aesop, the ancient Greek fabulist, mocked human folly through animal tales.

clue.text: Independent reserved?

explanation.surface: Asking whether someone independent is also reserved.
explanation.definitionFit: Private can mean not run by the state (independent) and also kept for particular people (reserved).

clue.text: No broad-spectrum drug?

parts.note: a medicine aimed at one particular disease rather than many

explanation.surface: Asking about a narrowly targeted medicine.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine, a specific is a remedy for one particular ailment.

clue.text: Multiply without going forth?

parts.note: reproducing within a closed group, never going outside it for a mate

explanation.surface: A biblical-sounding command to multiply, but staying put.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on 'go forth and multiply'.
explanation.definitionFit: To inbreed is to mate closely related individuals.

clue.text: Brings up short wickets

explanation.surface: Something stops a cricketer at the short wickets.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the stumps are the three upright sticks of the wicket.
explanation.definitionFit: To stump someone is to baffle them; stumps are also the uprights of a cricket wicket.

clue.text: An insurrection coming into being

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, A
a rising is a revolt or insurrection

explanation.surface: A revolt in the making.
explanation.definitionFit: Arising means emerging or coming into existence.

clue.text: Basic personality with endless character in Dostoevsky novel

parts.note: in Freud the id is the primitive part of the personality

indicators.note: endless means the final letter of the word is lost

parts.note: iota is a Greek letter or character

explanation.surface: A character analysis of someone in a Russian novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' takes the last A off IOTA, leaving IOT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Idiot is the 1869 novel by Fyodor Dostoevsky about Prince Myshkin.

clue.text: A time given to practice in home ground

indicators.note: given to means the following pieces are attached to the end of the practice

parts.note: a habit is a regular practice

explanation.surface: Time spent practising on one's home ground.
explanation.definitionFit: A habitat is the natural home environment of an animal or plant.

clue.text: The seat of government, silver in colour

indicators.note: in means the silver goes inside the colour

parts.note: a hue is a colour
Ag is the chemical symbol for silver

explanation.surface: A government building painted silver.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hague is where the Dutch government sits, though Amsterdam is the capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The Netherlands' parliament and government are based in The Hague.

clue.text: Drawing of beasts that attracts the opposite sex?

explanation.surface: A sketch of animals that turns out to be alluring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' is not a picture but a pull: magnetism, belonging to beasts.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally the magnetic pull of animals; figuratively raw sexual charm.

clue.text: Course taken from centre, exactly

indicators.note: taken from means the letters are lifted out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A course taken from the exact middle.
explanation.definitionFit: An entrée is a dish served as a course of a meal.

clue.text: Superfluous features off Isle of Wight, to the south

indicators.note: to the south means the S comes after, below in direction

parts.note: the Needles are chalk stacks off the western tip of the Isle of Wight

explanation.surface: Landmarks off the Isle of Wight, lying to the south.
explanation.walkthrough: The Needles are a famous row of chalk rocks off the Isle of Wight, an island off England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Needless means unnecessary, more than required.
